searchText: > In principle this is not a big issue Why don't you think it's too serious? The IGNORE rule only prevents the duplicate envelope, not the actual attack, or an I missing something? the 49/51 split still goes through and breaks canonicity of the next slot. Unless we're assuming all broadcasts propagate uniformly? Would this issue be solved by requiring the PTC to recompute the execution block hash before voting `payload_present=True`, without fully executing the payload? My understanding is that the execution `block_hash` is computed as `keccak256(rlp(header))`, where the header commits to fields such as `transactions_root` etc . So the PTC would not need to execute the transactions; it would only need to reconstruct the header commitments from the received payload/envelope and check: computed_block_hash == payload.block_hash == bid.block_hash If that check passed before voting, then a payload whose declared `payload.block_hash` matches the bid but whose actual contents hash to something else would not receive a positive timeliness vote. Am I missing any reason why this check is too expensive or insufficient for the PTC deadline? Generically, this would be the first time the consensus specs required RLP hashing of this sort Whether one things this is a blocking issue is subjective, but it's certainly not a minor one I see. Yeah I was just wondering because if this attack can be placed ‘easily’, then it’s quite bad. For instance without additional assumptions on the honesty of the previous slot builder, some properties would break. That’s why I was asking why it’s not a big issue Doing the rlp hash will still be irrelevant probably. The builder can invalidate other parts of the timely Payload Ah nvm everything else may be covered by the hash I'm too sleepy And I myself wrote the issue 🙂 But I believe this issue is definitely something to solve! The proofs are too sketchy (for now) to show where they break but we are planning to improve them soon. For what I can see, canonicity might break 😵 can't we simply add a gossip check for this, that does the rlp validation? "simply" For the record, Nimbus does check RLP in opt sync scenarios. But it's not a simple addition what proofs? you mean your document? yeah definitely they must be wrong if they do not account for payload equivocation. The reason I believe that the builder can't really trigger this off so easily is that they need to maintain a tight control over the gossip network: 1) They need exactly 49% of the PTC to get the invalid payload first. 2) They need exactly 51% of the attesters to get the valid payload first. 3) They need to get the proposer to be in the first set. 4) They need to do this with the payloads being quite separated in time to trigger this. I believe the combination of these events is impossible to trigger and Ethereum keeps almost-breaking the ability to do so by not providing the necessary information from the EL side blocks to properly replicate the EL blockhashes so if people actually want this isn't in no way "simple" and it requires cross-layer coordination So I think you guys may be exaggerating, but yes, it's worth analyzing what can come out of this, I believe ex-antee reorgs are far fetched, but perhaps some other form of attack that I can't see right now which is why I pinged Francesco Cayman wants to do the same to improve our optimistic sync like, every fork we have to check whether they break it and it's typically close and sometimes we've had to get spec tweaks in to help yeah it's a good feature anyway, I'll stop spamming. but <@586161934425128960> <@1040474166400405504> this is just not simple, it's a big big ask to put this in CL specs I'll be very against requiring RLP on CL clients and for us presumably it would be the easiest cause we can probably just import geth you know what would help here, is making EL blocks SSZ. then it would be simple to be clear, I don't like RLP on the CL side, but if that's what it takes didn't your EIP to get rid of payload sync suggest that too? Yes, the proofs do not yet account for a few aspects and are still quite sketchy at this stage. That said, I also believe that some effects of builder equivocation may be mitigated by the underlying network assumptions. For example, is it reasonable to assume that broadcasts (all broadcasts) propagate sufficiently uniformly across the network? Or it isn’t a fair assumption? In any case, I agree that this attack requires substantial power on the builder’s side. Nevertheless, if it does not violate any of the assumptions, then it represents a valid attack vector and should be addressed. I’m not really the best person here for advocating for something like this 🙉 so I trust your judgment.. I wanted first to think of a theoretical solution Again, just to be very clear: how does the builder manage to trigger a **different** split between the PTC set and the attester set? Already the fact that a very sophisticated actor can control a single split among all nodes is a bit far fetched, but have it so granular so as to identify exactly the nodes on the PTC and having them getting a different split than the attesters while **also** holding the exact percentage of the PTC of their own, it's black magic yes, I would definitely include it in CL clients if I get the benefit of not having to deal with payloads at all, but doing it for this issue there is no freaking way. As with any other spec addition: the risk of adding a bug in the addition needs to outweigh it's benefit. So, the typical assumption we make is that the builder/proposer has absolute control over which percentage of the chain gets its payload/block at a given timeline. Which is stronger (as in we assume more control from the builder) than the assumption you mention, therefore the protocol is stronger in that it should resist such control. However, this attack requires a strictly stronger assumption: that the builder can create and control different splits among different nodes that are randomly sampled from the p2p network! Interesting. Ok yes definitely stronger… I need to spend some time on this, but this is very helpful thanks!

excerpts.author: luca_zanolini
excerpts.content:
> In principle this is not a big issue

Why don't you think it's too serious? The IGNORE rule only prevents the duplicate envelope, not the actual attack, or an I missing something? the 49/51 split still goes through and breaks canonicity of the next slot. Unless we're assuming all broadcasts propagate uniformly?

excerpts.author: luca_zanolini
excerpts.content:
Would this issue be solved by requiring the PTC to recompute the execution block hash before voting `payload_present=True`, without fully executing the payload?

My understanding is that the execution `block_hash` is computed as `keccak256(rlp(header))`, where the header commits to fields such as `transactions_root` etc . So the PTC would not need to execute the transactions; it would only need to reconstruct the header commitments from the received payload/envelope and check:

computed_block_hash == payload.block_hash == bid.block_hash

If that check passed before voting, then a payload whose declared `payload.block_hash` matches the bid but whose actual contents hash to something else would not receive a positive timeliness vote.

Am I missing any reason why this check is too expensive or insufficient for the PTC deadline?

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content:
what proofs? you mean your document? yeah definitely they must be wrong if they do not account for payload equivocation. The reason I believe that the builder can't really trigger this off so easily is that they need to maintain a tight control over the gossip network:
1) They need exactly 49% of the PTC to get the invalid payload first.
2) They need exactly 51% of the attesters to get the valid payload first. 
3) They need to get the proposer to be in the first set. 
4) They need to do this with the payloads being quite separated in time to trigger this. 
I believe the combination of these events is impossible to trigger

Yes, the proofs do not yet account for a few aspects and are still quite sketchy at this stage. That said, I also believe that some effects of builder equivocation may be mitigated by the underlying network assumptions. In any case, I agree that this attack requires substantial power on the builder’s side. Nevertheless, if it does not violate any of the assumptions, then it represents a valid attack vector and should be addressed.
